content: The University of Buckingham is one of only two private universities in the United Kingdom, the other being Richmond University. It has gained significant recognition in recent years, having been ranked first for two consecutive years in the National Student Survey, which measures student satisfaction across the UK. The university operates two campuses located in Buckingham, Buckinghamshire, approximately 20 miles northeast of Oxford and 15 miles west of Milton Keynes. One campus is primarily dedicated to the study of Law, while the other, situated along the riverside in the town center, focuses on Business, Humanities, and Science disciplines. Buckingham is unique in the UK as it is the only university that operates independently of direct government funding. Among its notable academics are philosopher Roger Scruton, educationalist Alan Smithers, historian John Adamson, biographer Jane Ridley, and former Chief Inspector of Schools Chris Woodhead. The university was founded by academics who left the University of Oxford in the late 1960s, disillusioned with the prevailing ethos of the time. On May 27, 1967, Dr. J.W. Paulley published a letter in The Times proposing the establishment of a university modeled after the great private foundations in the United States. This idea led to three London conferences exploring the concept, and the university was subsequently incorporated as the University College of Buckingham in 1973. It received its Royal Charter from Queen Elizabeth II in 1983. The university's development was influenced by the libertarian Institute of Economic Affairs, particularly through the contributions of Harry Ferns and Ralph Harris. Reflecting its libertarian philosophy, the university's foundation stone was laid by Margaret Thatcher, who later served as its Chancellor from 1993 to 1998. The first two Vice-Chancellors were Lord Beloff and Sir Alan Peacock, both distinguished academics and prominent libertarians. The main campus is located in the historic county town of Buckingham, nestled within a bend of the River Ouse. It features a mix of 17th, 18th, and 19th-century buildings alongside modern teaching facilities. Some student residences are situated in scenic locations along the river. The Tanlaw Mill, a large historic building by the river, serves as a social hub for students, offering bars, a gym, a café, and other amenities. The modern Clore Laboratory, the elegant Hunter Street, and the administrative hub at Yeomanry House are also located on this campus. The Antony de Rothschild Building, overlooking the river, houses the Department of International Studies and Economics. Across the river, the Chandos Building includes large lecture theaters, language and media suites, exam halls, and gallery spaces. The university's second main campus is located uphill, closer to the town's edge, and features a central brick building that was formerly a convent. The university has four main faculties: Law, Humanities, Business, and Science. Its teaching approach is renowned for its continuation of the tutorial system, a tradition brought over from the University of Oxford. This method emphasizes small group teaching, typically involving 4 to 8 students with one staff member, allowing for a highly personalized learning experience. The staff-to-student ratio is 1:10, placing it among the highest in the UK. The university adheres to rigorous academic standards, with external examiners overseeing assessments, guidance from an Academic Advisory Council, and compliance with the Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education (QAA). Buckingham offers traditional degrees but over a shorter timeframe, with students completing 8 terms over two years instead of the usual 9 terms over three years. This accelerated structure, combined with reduced living expenses and earlier entry into the workforce, makes its programs cost-effective. As of September 2008, tuition fees for full-time UK/EU undergraduate students were £6,030 per year for the two-year Bachelor's degree programs. The university's research strengths span several diverse areas. In Law, it focuses on family law and gender-related legal issues. In Humanities, it is known for its work on Charles Dickens, including the Dickens Journals Online (DJO) project, as well as biography and life-writing. In Business, it specializes in entrepreneurship, while in Science, it conducts significant research on diabetes, obesity, and metabolic disorders at the Clore Laboratory, as well as face recognition systems within Computer Sciences. The Centre for Education and Employment Research, led by Alan Smithers and Dr. Pamela Robinson, investigates the state of education for policymakers and practitioners, with its reports frequently featured in the national press. The Dickens Journals Online project provides free access to a complete online edition of Dickens's weekly magazines, offering a rich resource of 19th-century literature, opinion, and history. The Denning Law Journal, edited by Professor Susan Edwards, is published by the university's Law faculty. The university was established as a liberal arts college in the spirit of North American Ivy League institutions. It offers major humanities subjects such as History and Politics, often combined with Economics in its International Studies degree. Economics is also available as a standalone degree, as are English Literature and combined degrees related to Journalism. Professor Martin Ricketts, the Dean of Humanities and Professor of Economics, chairs the Academic Advisory Council of the Institute of Economic Affairs, further strengthening the ties between the two libertarian institutions. The largest school at the university is Law, followed by Humanities, Business Studies, and Accounting. Some science departments, such as Biology, focus heavily on research and offer only research degrees, while others, such as Psychology and Computer Sciences, provide a full range of degree programs. The School of Law has been recognized for its excellence, achieving a top 20 ranking in the Guardian league tables. The university maintains close ties with international institutions, including the Sarajevo School of Science and Technology in Bosnia. It has also established a postgraduate medical school under the leadership of Professor Karol Sikora, with the first intake for the MD in Clinical Medicine expected in September 2008. The Department of Education includes prominent educationalists such as Professor Chris Woodhead, Professor Anthony O'Hear, and Professor Alan Smithers. Its Postgraduate Certificate in Education (PGCE), which specializes in the independent sector, has recently been accredited with Qualified Teacher Status (QTS), enabling graduates to teach in the state sector. Notable alumni include Richard Ballerand, Bader Ben Hirsi, Susanne Klatten, Brandon Lewis, and Olagunsoye Oyinlola. In a humorous nod, John Lloyd, host of the BBC Radio 4 panel game The Museum of Curiosity, claims to be the Professor of Ignorance at the University of Buckingham. Prominent author V.M. Xavier also presented special cultural performances at student functions in the 1980s. The university awards undergraduate and graduate degrees, including MBAs, to students who have studied at the European School of Economics. The current Chancellor of the University of Buckingham is Sir Martin Jacomb, who is also the Chairman of Canary Wharf Group PLC and Share PLC, as well as a director of several other companies, including the Oxford Playhouse Trust. He previously served as Chairman of Prudential PLC and retired from the boards of Rio Tinto PLC and Marks & Spencer PLC. Former Chancellors include Margaret Thatcher, who retired in 1999, and Lord Hailsham of St Marylebone. The current Vice-Chancellor is Dr. Terence Kealey, a clinical biochemistry specialist, who has held the position since April 2001. The University of Buckingham Press publishes works in the fields of law, education, and business through journal articles, books, reports, and other materials.
